articles.title: Japan space probe changes target over engine trouble
articles.summary: A Japanese probe that returned precious asteroid dust to Earth six years ago has changed course in its extended mission, officials said Tuesday, citing issues in its aging engines.

articles.title: Humpback whale snot unlocks whole-genome sequencing without invasive sampling
articles.summary: New research from the University of St Andrews, in collaboration with the University of Copenhagen, the North Coast Cetacean Society and Fisheries and Oceans Canada, has sequenced a whole whale genome using samples of "whale snot" collected by small drones off the coast of British Columbia—a world first.

articles.title: Tossing Fireworks from Cloud to Cloud
articles.summary: For many astronauts, the spectacular sight of lightning stands out when looking back at Earth from the International Space Station.

articles.title: The sun, Earth, Jupiter and white dwarfs: Potential traps for dark matter
articles.summary: Dark matter continues to evade direct detection. Its slower-moving particles might leave signals too faint for detectors to register, yet be more easily captured by planets and stars. As they accumulate inside these bodies, they could produce effects that existing instruments would allow us to search for.

articles.title: What makes food 'organic?' For many consumers, the answer isn't always on the label
articles.summary: "Organic" is a word we encounter every time we visit the supermarket. It's also one that can mean very different things to different people.

articles.title: Report finds consistent pandemic learning loss and gaps between grades and test scores across Canada
articles.summary: A new national report identifies declines in student performance in every province and territory examined in Canada, with grade inflation obscuring the extent of setbacks during the COVID-19 pandemic.

articles.title: Mourning Notcho: What one whale's death teaches us about ecological grief
articles.summary: Sighting a humpback whale from a boat can be awe-inspiring. For some BC Ferries passengers, that experience became disturbing when their ferry struck and fatally injured a humpback whale on Oct. 18.

articles.title: How enhanced rock weathering can speed up carbon capture
articles.summary: Water flooded the pasture, spilling from an irrigation pipe tucked alongside a hill at the Sierra Foothill Research and Extension Center, a University of California research facility located about 20 miles (32 kilometers) east of Yuba City. For more than three hours, starting at 6 a.m. this summer day, the water had seeped into the soils beneath the yellow-green grass, spreading to various depths while flowing downslope toward its destination.

articles.title: Could your personality be affecting how you feel about social media?
articles.summary: Social media offers everyone the same basic promise: post something about yourself and get responses from other people. Whether it's a vacation, a promotion or just a midweek meal, these days many people's lives are shared online.

articles.title: Baby, she's back: SpaceX catches a Starship from orbit for first time
articles.summary: SpaceX brought back its Starship rocket's second stage today for a first-ever midair capture at its launch pad, capping a record-setting orbital flight test.

articles.title: Flat optics roadmap charts path toward smaller imaging and sensing systems
articles.summary: For centuries, optical systems have relied on lenses, mirrors and other components that manipulate light through their shape and size. Today, advances in nanotechnology are enabling a different approach. Researchers can now engineer materials at scales smaller than the wavelength of light, creating ultrathin optical components that offer new ways to control how light behaves.

articles.title: Early black holes may have grown through productive chaos
articles.summary: When the universe was less than 700 million years old, the supermassive black hole powering a quasar called J0313-1806 had already grown to about 3 billion times the mass of the sun. It is one of the most extreme examples of a puzzle that has occupied astrophysicists for two decades: How did supermassive black holes grow so big so quickly?

articles.title: 'Buffer spaces' may help resolve workplace concerns
articles.summary: Nearly every person will run into conflict in their workplace at some point in their career, but it can be difficult to know when or how to report these concerns.

articles.title: AI could help speed up research ethics approvals
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence programs could be used to improve efficiency for professionals dealing with research ethics reviews, enabling humans to focus on the ethical decision-making.

articles.title: Flip side: Upside-down atomic layers could steer heat in stacked computer chips
articles.summary: Stacking chips on top of one another could keep computers getting faster, but it creates a heating problem. Now, researchers from Japan have found that simply flipping atom-thin layers upside down could help steer that heat where it needs to go.

articles.title: New analysis shows that even young children want to be seen as morally good
articles.summary: As early as 130,000 years ago, the first human societies were built on morality and cooperation within groups. The same is true today. Even young children exhibit a distinctly human desire to be seen as morally good. That is the conclusion of a new article by researchers at Leipzig University. Humboldt Research Fellow Dr. Leon Li and Junior Professor Dr. Sebastian Grüneisen are investigating the origins of human cooperation and social identity. Their paper, "Evolutionary foundations of social identity," has just been published in the journal Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.

articles.title: Tigers, zebras, quantum dots: Nanoparticles assemble into patterns
articles.summary: Forget about how the zebra got its stripes. For a group of Cornell engineers, an equally important question is: What drives the formation of such eye-catching patterns?

articles.title: Capping nanovials that trap cells and their secretions for analysis enables new bioscience experiments
articles.summary: A UCLA-developed technology that is like a test tube but on the cellular scale has led to a number of biomedical discoveries in recent years, including revelations about cancer, heart disease and the genetic levers that push cells to release proteins.

articles.title: Researchers are testing whether agrivoltaics can help farmers adapt to hotter, drier conditions
articles.summary: Majdi Abou Najm stands in a tomato crop under the summer sun in UC Davis' agricultural research fields. A few hours after sunrise, the sun is beginning to feel less like warmth and more like a weight—the kind of heat that could scald tomatoes on the vine.

articles.title: Euclid's H-alpha observations map where stars form in distant galaxies
articles.summary: Euclid was launched into space in July 2023 to explore two of astronomy's biggest mysteries: dark matter and dark energy. The space telescope's first major data release covers some 1,900 square degrees of the sky, equivalent to around 14% of the area planned for the six-year mission and around 5% of the total sky. It is an unprecedented collection of visible and near-infrared observations.

articles.title: Long-term study reveals how humidity affects the durability of biodegradable thermoplastic polymers
articles.summary: As the demand for sustainable alternatives to conventional plastics continues to grow, biodegradable polymers such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA) are attracting increasing attention for applications ranging from packaging to consumer products.

articles.title: Tiny switch harnesses four electrical states, moving beyond simple on-off control
articles.summary: From light switches to transistors, many kinds of switches have exactly two states: on or off, conducting or insulating, zero or one. Researchers at TU Wien are working with unusual materials that challenge some of the standard assumptions of materials physics. Using one of these materials, they have developed a tiny switch with four distinct states and several ways to move between them. This opens up new ways to process and store information. The study is published in the journal Communications Materials.

articles.title: Turning biomass into renewable fuels and chemicals using microorganisms
articles.summary: Texas A&M University researchers have developed a process that converts biomass into renewable fuels and chemicals. Dr. Mark Holtzapple, professor in the Artie McFerrin Department of Chemical Engineering, aims to make producing these products more efficient and affordable by using microorganisms to break down plant material.

articles.summary: Written by Candice Bedford, Research Scientist at Purdue University Date: Nov. 16, 2026 During the Perseverance rover’s investigation of “Idubi” — an area of ancient Martian crust exposed in the “Lac de Charmes” region, outside of Jezero crater — the Perseverance rover team has been captivated by a cluster of eerily bright, light-toned rocks in […]

articles.title: AI tool counts mosquito eggs in smartphone photos to aid surveillance
articles.summary: Your mission, should you choose to accept it: Track down and identify thousands of nearly microscopic mosquito eggs hiding in plain sight. Your only weapon? A smartphone armed with artificial intelligence.

articles.title: Sunspot dynamic fibrils linked to slow magnetoacoustic waves
articles.summary: Using high-resolution observations from the New Vacuum Solar Telescope (NVST), a research team from the Yunnan Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) has systematically studied the kinematic properties of dynamic fibrils around a sunspot and the mechanisms that drive them. The study was published in The Astrophysical Journal on Nov. 10.

articles.title: Ultracold diamond microwave laser amplifies quantum signals 1,000-fold
articles.summary: Researchers from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have created a spin-based microwave amplifier that operates near absolute zero, boosting signals by more than 1,000-fold while adding noise close to the bare minimum required by the laws of physics. As a more robust alternative to current state-of-the-art devices, the OIST device can handle much stronger signals and operate in magnetic fields, paving the way for practical quantum computing and higher-resolution sensing technologies.

articles.title: Why marine climate refugia matter for safeguarding the world's oceans
articles.summary: The ocean is changing rapidly. Warming, acidification, oxygen loss, sea-level rise and the intensification of extreme events are transforming marine ecosystems, leading to species shifts and mass mortality events. However, these impacts are not distributed evenly. There are areas that buffer these effects and act as true "marine climate refugia."

articles.title: Two gorillas form a 'living ladder' to reach high branches
articles.summary: Observations by a team of researchers from Tel Aviv University at the Ramat Gan Safari reveal recurring cooperation between two adult female gorillas, who assume complementary roles to solve a practical problem.

articles.title: The expanding genetics of blue eyes in cats
articles.summary: Blue eyes in cats have long attracted attention, especially when they occur in cats with fully colored coats. The dominant blue eye (DBE) phenotype has become increasingly visible across several breeds. When we prepared our literature review, four independent DBE variants had been described in scientific publications. Today, eight variants are reported, although published genetic evidence is available for six. Some of these variants are also associated with health concerns.

articles.title: Can AI replace college advisers? Research says not yet
articles.summary: Colleges use AI tools for academic advising, analyzing data to predict which students need additional help. But research from Princeton Engineering suggests that helping students requires judgment and expertise that go beyond the algorithm.

articles.title: A Collage Showing 49 Drill Holes Made by NASA’s Curiosity Mars Rover
articles.summary: Description This collage shows 49 drill holes captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover as of November 2026. Each hole represents a sample collected from rocks on the Martian surface; Curiosity’s drill, located on the end of its robotic arm, drops pulverized rock samples into instruments in its belly that analyze their composition. These images were […]

articles.title: COP 31: Who qualifies for loss and damage funding? Why country borders are a poor guide
articles.summary: Developing countries hardest hit by climate change were promised a new source of support when governments agreed at the annual global climate change conference in 2022 (COP27) to create a Loss and Damage fund. This fund was intended to help them cope with losses ranging from destroyed homes and livelihoods to the loss of lives and cultural heritage.

articles.title: NASA Receives 16th Consecutive ‘Clean’ Financial Audit Opinion
articles.summary: For the 16th consecutive year, NASA has received an unmodified, or “clean,” opinion from an external auditor on its fiscal year 2026 financial statements. The rating is the best possible audit opinion, certifying that NASA’s financial statements conform with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles for federal agencies and accurately present the agency’s financial position. “Our responsibility […]

articles.title: Sentinel-6B in Orbit Around Earth
articles.summary: Description This artist’s concept shows the Sentinel-6B satellite, which will become the reference satellite for other missions studying sea surface height.

articles.title: Thunderbirds in Formation
articles.summary: U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds fighter jets pass overhead during the agency’s MAX POWER expo and air show on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. NASA’s inaugural MAX POWER was an aerospace festival celebrating the past, present, and future of flight and space exploration in honor of America’s 250th anniversary. Image […]

articles.title: Contractor to Civil Servant: NASA Welcomes Jim Mirandy
articles.summary: The rumble of a rocket engine might be considered a soundtrack for Jim Mirandy’s life. Mirandy has grown up with NASA as a constant presence, and his path to becoming a civil servant at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, has been decades in the making. Hired under the agency’s workforce directive […]

articles.title: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
articles.summary: Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.

articles.title: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that the heart ages unevenly, with surprising hotspots of inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than the heart muscle. The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about cardiac aging and could help researchers develop new ways to protect the heart as we grow older.

articles.title: NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base
articles.summary: NASA is offering $1 million in its new Moon Base Challenge, inviting U.S. students to develop innovative solutions for building humanity’s first permanent lunar outpost. From power systems to astronaut safety, their ideas could help make long-term life on the Moon possible and pave the way to Mars.

articles.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world
articles.summary: A European spacecraft has revealed a mysterious, crater-covered side of the asteroid Didymos as it prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact. The mission could uncover new clues about the collision and help turn asteroid deflection into a powerful defense against future threats to Earth.

articles.title: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain
articles.summary: New research reveals that biological sex, genetics, and menopause may dramatically influence Alzheimer's risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. Scientists also uncovered surprising differences in immune activity and gut-brain interactions, opening the door to more personalized treatments for neurological disorders.

articles.title: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
articles.summary: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud. These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining for valuable metals.

articles.title: A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death
articles.summary: A surprising new study suggests that when and how often older adults nap could reveal hidden warning signs about their health. Researchers followed 1,338 people for up to 19 years and discovered that longer, more frequent naps were linked to higher mortality, while morning nappers faced a 30% greater risk of death than afternoon nappers. Each additional hour of daytime sleep was associated with a 13% increase in mortality risk.

articles.title: New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery
articles.summary: A revolutionary new wearable patch could help people get more restorative sleep without medication or surgery. Developed by University of Texas researchers, the device uses gentle ultrasound to stimulate deep brain regions, helping participants enter REM sleep 43 minutes faster and remain there 16 minutes longer on average. The technology also showed promising effects on stress regulation and brain circuits involved in emotion.

articles.title: The Last Ice on Puncak Jaya
articles.summary: Ice near the summit of the Indonesian mountain peak has shrunk to scattered patches too small to flow like glaciers.

articles.title: The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets
articles.summary: Scientists have turned the thin plastic used in emergency blankets into remarkably strong insulation that could help astronauts survive the Moon's extreme temperatures. Built from hundreds of stacked layers, the material withstands crushing pressure without losing its thermal protection, potentially paving the way for tougher, longer-lasting lunar habitats.

articles.title: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom
articles.summary: Scientists have unexpectedly discovered how to control the magnetic spin inside a single atom's nucleus using radio waves, overturning previous assumptions about atomic behavior. The breakthrough could pave the way for more reliable quantum memory, although researchers are still trying to understand why it works.

articles.title: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
articles.summary: MIT scientists discovered that carefully timed bursts of gentle pink noise during sleep can strengthen the brain’s natural cleaning waves, which help flush away potentially harmful waste. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments aimed at improving sleep and memory while potentially reducing the buildup of proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease.

articles.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
articles.summary: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.

articles.title: Giant, prehistoric rodent fossils discovered in southern Thailand
articles.summary: An international team of paleontologists, including researchers from McGill University, has discovered "remarkably large" rodent fossils in the pit of a mine in southern Thailand. The finding, published in Scientific Reports, provides a new perspective on the early manifestation of rodent gigantism—the process by which animals evolve to become larger—demonstrating that the evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents is considerably older and more geographically widespread than previously recognized, the researchers said.

articles.title: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that vitamin C may help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming in the stomach after eating foods containing nitrates and nitrites. A new mathematical model suggests that taking vitamin C after meals could reduce these harmful reactions, offering a possible new strategy for lowering cancer risk.

articles.title: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising genetic connection to spinal degeneration and found that an existing osteoporosis drug can prevent damaging mineral buildup in zebrafish spines. The discovery could pave the way for new treatments that slow or prevent a major cause of chronic back pain.

articles.title: New observations challenge evidence for an 'outsize' black hole in the early universe
articles.summary: A recent reanalysis of the outsize black hole galaxy UHZ1 using existing X-ray data and new infrared observations challenges a previous groundbreaking claim. Three years ago, this galaxy made news for hosting an unusually massive and heavily dust-obscured black hole formed through direct collapse. Led by Fan Zou of the University of Michigan, the new study reports no signs of hidden black hole activity. The paper, published in The Astrophysical Journal on Oct. 14, suggests UHZ1 could be a low-mass, metal-poor, star-forming galaxy.

articles.title: NASA warns this year's Monster El Niño could be even bigger than legendary 1997 event
articles.summary: NASA scientists warn that the rapidly intensifying 2026 El Niño could surpass the historic 1997-98 event, which triggered devastating weather extremes around the world. Satellite data reveal striking similarities between the two, raising the possibility of major rainfall and flooding this winter, although the exact impacts remain uncertain.

articles.title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained
articles.summary: The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields. Remarkably, the models indicate that their magnetic poles could shift by tens of degrees within just a few decades, far faster than Earth's.

articles.title: Taiwan Indigenous farmer revives climate-resilient millet
articles.summary: Indigenous farmer Banu Ismahasan walks through a golden field of tall stalks in southeastern Taiwan, harvesting by hand the grain heads of an ancient crop resistant to extreme weather.

articles.title: Nations grapple with loss of 1.5C target at UN climate summit
articles.summary: For a decade, the 1.5C goal has served as the north star of climate action, a line nations pledged to hold to avoid the worst ravages of a warming planet.

articles.title: SpaceX's Starship returns from orbit and is captured by launch pad arms in a dramatic first
articles.summary: SpaceX's Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

articles.title: Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange stellar pair more than 5,000 light-years away, where a dead star spinning every eight minutes produces mysterious radio pulses while orbiting a Sun-like star. The breakthrough also revealed massive magnetic storms on the companion star, offering fresh clues to one of astronomy's emerging mysteries.

articles.title: ALMA reveals three star-forming cores at different stages inside one gas clump
articles.summary: Astronomers have revealed three dense cores at different evolutionary stages within the massive star-forming region G40.282−0.219, shedding light on the physical and chemical differences among cores within the same massive dense clump.

articles.title: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections
articles.summary: A surprising discovery from Rockefeller University suggests that a common amino acid could play a powerful role in protecting against cancer and viral infections. Scientists found that low arginine levels interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize dangerous cells, while increasing arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice. Even more remarkably, giving mice arginine after they contracted influenza helped them recover.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
articles.summary: Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a powerful new way to identify people at risk.

articles.title: Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins
articles.summary: A groundbreaking drone survey has revealed a startling split in the fate of New Zealand's endangered Erect-crested penguins. While one population has remained stable for decades, another has declined by more than 40%, apparently due to a combination of predators, worsening storms, and changing ocean conditions. Even more surprisingly, the tiny Bounty Islands support nearly as many breeding pairs as the Antipodes Islands, despite being 40 times smaller.

articles.title: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago
articles.summary: Dinosaurs may have been snacking on seaweed and other ocean foods more than 100 million years ago, according to surprising new evidence hidden in their fossilized teeth. Researchers discovered chemical signatures suggesting that coastal dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals relied partly on nutrients originating in the sea. The findings reveal that marine resources traveled through ancient food chains, supplementing the diets of everything from plant-eating dinosaurs to predators.

articles.title: Physicists use laser light to unlock a crystal's hidden electrical powers
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered how to use flashes of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions inside a crystal, solving a decades-old mystery about how the material behaves. The laser-induced alignment lasts just a trillionth of a second, but the breakthrough could open the door to new ways of processing and storing information.

articles.title: Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns
articles.summary: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 ancient quasars, including two record-breaking objects that shone with the brightness of a trillion Suns when the Universe was just 670 million years old. Powered by supermassive black holes, these extraordinary cosmic beacons reveal a time when the first galaxies were still taking shape.

articles.title: Is this iconic black hole image accurate? New study delivers an independent result
articles.summary: On April 10, 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) Collaboration revealed the first picture of a black hole. The object is at the center of a galaxy known as M87, about 55 million light-years away.

articles.title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.

articles.title: Urban expansion causes ecological collapse in streams in the São Paulo Metropolitan Area
articles.summary: The advance of urbanization in the São Paulo Metropolitan Area in Brazil is causing the collapse of food webs in local streams. A study published in August in the journal Nature Cities reveals that the impact of the metropolis goes far beyond a simple reduction in species. Degradation selectively eliminates organisms based on their size and simplifies ecological interactions. Networks of 190 connections plummet to just three.

articles.title: A dead star is flashing radio waves every 8 minutes, and its partner looks a lot like the sun
articles.summary: Since 2022, astronomers have been puzzling over a new kind of cosmic object called long-period radio transients. These are objects that emit bright flashes of radio waves into space every few minutes to every few hours. Some have been traced back to binary systems consisting of a small, dim, cool star called a red dwarf in orbit with a stellar remnant called a white dwarf.

articles.title: Does your culture shape how you look at art? What an eye‑tracking study in Sudan revealed
articles.summary: Today, Old Dongola is an abandoned settlement on the banks of the Nile in northern Sudan. Hundreds of years ago, however, this place looked very different.

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 closes in on a light-day in interstellar space for a new distance record
articles.summary: NASA's Voyager 1 is about to become humanity's first object to reach one light-day from Earth as it pushes ever deeper into interstellar space.

articles.title: A cosmic magnifying glass could reveal the same supernova two more times in roughly 70 years
articles.summary: Thanks to the gravitational lensing caused by a massive galaxy cluster and high-resolution images from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers discovered an exploding star when the universe was 4.9 billion years old. The discovery paper, posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 23, presents a prediction for when the rest of the distorted images of SN Ares will arrive.

articles.title: Some of the oldest rocks ever discovered shed light on Earth's early history
articles.summary: Earth is approximately 4.5 billion years old, according to estimates. However, rocks dating back to the planet's earliest days are extremely rare. Hence the excitement over the discovery in northern China of some of the oldest known rocks on Earth, dating back 3.95 billion years. And one of the reasons for all the attention is that they're revealing new clues about how Earth's crust formed and evolved.

articles.title: World's largest freshwater lake is recovering after decades of decline
articles.summary: Lake Baikal in Siberia holds around 20% of the world's surface freshwater, making it the most voluminous freshwater lake (Lake Superior on the United States–Canada border is the largest by surface area). This makes the lake one of the most important environments for biodiversity—in fact, it was designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1996 because of this. Yet it has shown considerable decline over the last century, with aridification spreading across East Asia.
